This page treats preparation and cutting, heating and serving, and cleaning, storage and records as three overlapping work surfaces, not as three official subcategories or a uniform operating procedure. There are currently five subcategories with detailed profiles: fast food 20 tasks 15Core/5Supplemental, institution and cafeteria 17 tasks 12/5, private household 13 tasks 12/1, restaurant 20 tasks 14/6 and short order 11 tasks 8/3. The 35-2019 other cooks page explicitly does not provide that class of O*NET characteristic data, so it cannot be written that all six have detailed task and interest profiles. Importance is not frequency. Household menu design, institutional mentoring and restaurant coordination and supervision all have Core tasks, so management or menu work must not be uniformly excluded. Whether the menu, purchasing, special diets and mentoring fall to the cook must be checked against the specific subcategory and unit, not only the station operation.
Preparation and cutting

Check the menu and orders → receive ingredients and check shelf life by batch → weigh to the recipe and record the gram weights → wash, peel, cut and portion → isolate allergen-related ingredients → label the production time and batch
Preparation and portioning records, and allergen isolation confirmation
Heating and temperature control

Confirm equipment cleanliness and operating status → choose the heating method by order → control heat and time → check the core temperature with a thermometer → sensory check of doneness and taste → portion and plate and record temperature control data
Temperature control and production records, and anomaly stop-serving and reporting confirmation
Cleaning, storage and records

Clean and sanitise, rotate storage, verify output and stock and record anomalies to the applicable standards and unit procedures, and pass on outstanding items by the unit's handover method; O*NET tasks do not uniformly require all positions to sign in person.
Where is the boundary between cooks (the occupational family) and adjacent food service positions?

This table compares the cook family with adjacent food service positions item by item across seven dimensions: core purpose, main objects and basis, core process, main outputs, responsible party, cooperation and supervision, and conclusion boundary. Adjacent positions all work in food service or food preparation settings, but autonomy over the menu and dishes, whether personnel and cost management is carried, whether there is direct customer contact, and the food safety and temperature control chain of responsibility do not transfer just because the positions are adjacent; when comparing, check the position's actual duties item by item.
Core purpose
Prepare ingredients into safely edible finished dishes to the recipe and order, and reproduce the taste and portion consistently within the serving deadline.

Core purposes of adjacent positions: chefs and head cooks are responsible for menu design, kitchen organisation and production standards; food service managers are responsible for outlet operations, cost and personnel; food preparation workers are responsible for washing, cutting and other upstream preparation; bakers make baked products to recipe; fast food and counter workers take orders, assemble and hand over; dishwashers are responsible for cleaning tableware and premises.
Main objects and basis

Ingredients, recipes, orders and temperature control records; the basis is food safety requirements, menu and recipe standards, orders and the serving pace, and the employer's kitchen operating standards.

Objects and basis of adjacent positions: menus and cost sheets (chefs and managers), preparation lists and recipes (preparation workers), dough and baking recipes (bakers), cash register and order systems (counter workers), and tableware and cleaning processes (dishwashers).
Core process
Receiving and preparation → weighing, cutting and portioning → heating and temperature control by order → sensory and instrument checks → plating and serving → cleaning, storage and records.

Processes of adjacent positions: menu and cost accounting, scheduling and purchasing, washing and cutting and preparing, fermentation and baking, order assembly and payment, and cleaning, sanitising and returning items.
Main outputs
Dishes that can be reproduced consistently, serving records and temperature control data, and ingredient stock rotated on a first-in-first-out basis.

Outputs of adjacent positions: an accountable menu and gross margin, outlet operating reports, prepared semi-finished items, baked products, correct orders and payment, and clean tableware and premises.
Responsible party

Actual ingredient, processing, hygiene and record duties are checked per position, and food producers and business operators and their principal responsible persons bear the legal responsibility; cooks may also take on the menu, purchasing and mentoring. Equipment modification and repair are checked against authority, and no authority is conferred by the job title.

Adjacent management positions may take on operations and personnel management, but menu, purchasing or supervision are not exclusively theirs; household menu design and institutional mentoring are also core tasks for cook subcategories. Counter payment and dishwashing must be checked against the target position.
Cooperation and supervision

Work is divided by station within the kitchen, and at the serving peak the timing must be aligned with the plating assistant, the food runner and the front of house; when a temperature, foreign object or equipment anomaly is found, stop the affected work and report it to the supervisor.

Cooperation of adjacent positions: chefs and managers assign tasks and shifts; preparation workers receive the cook's specification requirements; counter workers check order changes with the kitchen; dishwashers share cleaning and storage space with the kitchen.
Conclusion boundary

Similar job titles do not mean interchangeability: whether the person designs dishes and the menu independently, manages people, money and goods, and faces customers directly determines the scope of authorization and where responsibility lies.

The preparation levels and qualification requirements of adjacent positions do not apply to this occupation and must be checked item by item against each occupation's official material and the employer's system.
Key occupational judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether the ingredient receiving and temperature control records are checked; whether cutting, preparing and portioning meet the recipe specification; whether the core temperature and doneness after heating are up to standard; whether allergens and cross-contamination are isolated; whether cleaning, sanitising and storage follow procedure; and whether anomalies are reported to procedure and handed over to the next shift.

Receiving must check the batch, shelf life and cold chain status and record the temperature to the shift's actual reading; receiving purely on appearance leaves later spoilage or temperature failure as a food safety risk.
Weighing, cutting and portioning must be carried out and re-checked to the recipe and gram requirements; estimating by feel makes taste, cost and portion size drift together.

Check doneness against the applicable temperature and time for the dish and the unit's procedure; sensory judgment is one of the restaurant tasks, and appearance, taste or tasting alone cannot prove that potentially contaminated food is safe. This round obtained no ranking of food safety hazard frequency.
Ingredients, utensils and stations containing allergens must be handled and labelled separately; using a shared station without cleaning passes the risk to customers who do not know about it.
Judgment four: are allergens and cross-contamination isolated?

Utensils and chopping boards must be handled to the cleaning and sanitising procedure, and ingredients stored and rotated on a first-in-first-out basis with the time labelled; skipping sanitising or putting new stock in front leaves the problem for the next shift.
Judgment five: do cleaning, sanitising and storage follow procedure?

When a temperature, foreign object or equipment anomaly is found, stop the affected work, isolate and escalate to the applicable procedure, and state clearly what has been handled and what still needs checking. Article 47 of the Chinese law provides that where there is a potential food safety incident the producer or business operator must stop production and operation and report to the regulatory department, so reporting only to the supervisor cannot replace the statutory report. The handover form follows the unit's rules.

Preparation and cutting | Receive ingredients and weigh and cut to recipe | Check ingredient freshness and storage temperature, weigh, wash, peel, cut and portion to the recipe, handle meat, seafood, vegetables and fruit, and isolate allergen-related ingredients as required.

Heating and serving | Heat by order and re-check doneness | Choose pan-frying, stir-frying, roasting, steaming, deep-frying and baking and similar methods to heat by order, adjust the temperature of stoves, ovens, grills and steamers, re-check doneness by tasting, smelling and piercing with an implement, and after portioning, plating and garnishing hand over to the food runner or directly to the customer.

Temperature control and hygiene | Monitor temperature and prevent cross-contamination | Monitor refrigeration, freezing, heating and holding temperatures to food safety requirements, record the key temperature control data, keep the preparation area, stations and serving area clean, clean and sanitise utensils and chopping boards to procedure and store raw and cooked ingredients separately.

Stock and records | Check stock and record truthfully | Take stock of and requisition ingredients and kitchen supplies, rotate storage on a first-in-first-out basis, record output, waste, temperature control and stock data, and report shortages, losses and anomalies to the supervisor.

Cooperation and supervision | Work with the kitchen crew and mentor newcomers | At the serving peak align the timing with the plating assistant, the food runner and the front of house, work by station, assist or cover for other cooks, and guide newly hired kitchen helpers and apprentices as arranged by the employer.

Safety and equipment | Use equipment to procedure and report faults | Use stoves, deep fryers, slicers and mixers and similar equipment to the employer's safety procedures, wear protective equipment and clean and maintain equipment promptly; when an equipment fault or a gas or electrical anomaly is found, stop using it and notify the supervisor.
Work context and working conditions

After service starts, prepare, heat and portion continuously by order, and when a temperature, foreign object or equipment anomaly appears, stop the affected work and report it; at close, clean the equipment, store ingredients on a first-in-first-out basis and record temperature control and stock.

Provide large-volume catering to a fixed population (schools, hospitals, companies, aged care facilities) according to the menu and dietary restrictions, and record food usage and temperature under the system.
Design menus, purchase and cook meals around the needs of a single household or a few employers, balancing dietary restrictions and family tastes, and possibly travelling with the employer.

Restaurant Cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2014.00)

Serve continuously to the menu and orders in a restaurant back kitchen: the dish range is wide and there are many stations, so the person must both reproduce taste to recipe and align serving timing with the plating assistant and the food runner at peak times.

Compared with the other subcategories in the family, restaurant cooks have the widest dish range and the most coordinating stations; employment in 2024 was 1,460,200, the largest subcategory in the family.
Better suited to people willing to coordinate serving in a high-pace, multi-dish environment and able to accept evening and weekend shifts.
Fast Food Cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2011.00)
Make in batches to order under standardised equipment and a fixed menu, with short processes, a fast pace and high repetition, and some positions also take orders and payment.

More constrained by standardised equipment and serving pace: employment in 2024 was 669,500, and 2024—2034 growth is a decline (-1% or lower), with automation and job consolidation more evident in fast food and counter positions.
Better suited to people who can accept a high degree of repetition, work to standards and want to start fairly quickly.
Institution and Cafeteria Cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2012.00)
Large volume, a fixed client population and relatively regular hours; employment in 2024 was 466,100, 2024—2034 growth is slower than average (1% to 2%), and the page does not mark Bright Outlook.
Better suited to people who value regular hours, batch catering and institutionalised management rather than pursuing dish creativity.
Private Household Cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2013.00)

High autonomy over the menu and purchasing, with the workplace in a private residence; employment in 2024 was 34,200, 2024—2034 growth is faster than average (5% to 6%), and the preparation level is Job Zone 3.
Better suited to people willing to deal directly with a single household, design menus themselves and adapt to family routines.
Short Order Cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-2015.00)
The shortest processes, with customer orders directly determining the order of production; employment in 2024 was 151,100, and 2024—2034 growth is a decline (-1% or lower).
Better suited to people who react quickly, can handle several short orders at once and face customers directly.
Chefs and Head Cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00, adjacent occupation)

The key difference from this occupation is management responsibility: taking on menu design and cost accounting, personnel scheduling and training, and setting production standards; these duties do not belong to the general positions in the cook family.
Better suited to people who have built production experience, are willing to take on personnel and cost management responsibility and want to lead the menu direction.

Sanitation and safety

Heating and seasoning
Season and cook by heating according to recipes or personal experience

Judging doneness
Observe and taste food to judge whether it is thoroughly cooked

A temperature probe is a measuring tool, not generative AI; check its calibration, the measurement point and the applicable limits, and sensory checks cannot replace the legally required heating conditions.

Verify system inputs
Check the source of order, recipe and inventory data and confirm that nothing has been overwritten or mismatched; input errors are amplified along the whole service chain.
Keep human review points
Keep human review for key judgements on allergens, temperature control, doneness and batch consistency, and do not replace on-site confirmation with system prompts.
Records and traceability
Record temperature control, cleaning and exception handling according to the employer's system, stating who reviewed them; records must be traceable to a specific shift.
Exception handling and stopping service

When abnormal temperatures, foreign objects, equipment faults or suspected allergen cross-contamination are found, stop the affected work and report it, and authorised personnel decide whether to discard or resume.
Training and authorisation
Operation, parameter adjustment and maintenance of tools must be performed by trained and authorised personnel; unverified suggestions must not replace operating procedures.

What are the actual work risks for cooks (occupational family)?

Risks cluster into three types: burns and cuts from heat and knives, injuries from wet and slippery surfaces and from lifting, and food-safety risks from temperature-control failures and cross-contamination; long-term heat, noise and repetitive motion also have cumulative effects.

Task hazards and work context are checked against the O*NET restaurant detail page, and food-safety and health requirements against the 2025 amendment to the Food Safety Law; the Chinese cuisine chef material supports classification grades only, and NIST is voluntary AI governance only. All back-of-house stations, especially frying, oven and slicing positions
When using frying equipment, ovens and slicers, excessively high oil temperature, contact between oil and water, improper blade orientation or missing guards can all cause burns and cuts.
Burns and cuts cause lost work and absence, and improper emergency handling may cause secondary injury.

Dishwashing areas, prep areas and cold-store lifting positions

All stations that come into direct contact with ingredients and finished dishes

Refrigeration and freezer temperature failures, shared chopping boards and utensils between cooked and raw food, and allergen information that is not isolated can all cause foodborne illness or allergic reactions in customers.
Food-safety incidents cause harm to customer health and business suspension and rectification, and individuals may bear corresponding responsibility.

values: Fictional work-order material (practice input)

Fictional scenario: a fictional restaurant receives three orders before Friday dinner service — one gluten-free pan-seared chicken breast with seasonal vegetables, two regular beef burger sets and one toddler meal (low salt, no nuts). The freezer temperature log shows an abnormal rise of 42 minutes around midday that day, and the shift record says only “handled”.

Material provided: the recipes and gram-weight requirements for the three orders; the shift's freezer and heating equipment temperature records; the ingredient batch and shelf-life ledger; the allergen ingredient list; a summary of the cleaning and disinfection procedure.

Material not provided: the specific cause of the abnormal temperature, whether the affected ingredients have already been used, the approval process for deciding whether to discard them, and the shift's staffing. If these conditions are needed in the exercise, state your assumptions and whom you would need to confirm them with.
Task requirements

Write a one-page shift handling and service plan covering order and allergen checks, the judgement and handling of the affected ingredients, heating and temperature-control requirements, portioning and plating arrangements, the situations that require stopping service or reporting, and the items to hand over to the next shift.
The plan must state which data come from the exercise material and which are still assumptions, and must say whether it relies on the recipe, the temperature-control records or the procedure summary.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the exercise material)

The plan should include: checks (label the allergens and dietary restrictions for each of the three orders separately, exclude nuts from the toddler meal and control salt); ingredient judgement (ingredients in the cabinet during the midday temperature anomaly must be held back from use and reported, and must not be released on the strength of a “handled” record alone); heating and temperature control (check the core temperature of the chicken breast and burger meat against the dish requirements); portioning and plating (dedicated allergen utensils and station isolation); exception handling (stop using the affected ingredients and report before the temperature anomaly is characterised, with authorised personnel deciding whether to discard or release them); records and handover (set out the period of the temperature anomaly, the batches involved, the action taken and the items still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; explaining the basis for your judgement is enough.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be drawn

This exercise tests only hygiene and temperature-control awareness, allergen checking and the ability to organise records; it does not evaluate the safety of a real kitchen and does not constitute a hiring or qualification judgement or advice on real food-safety handling.

Real restaurants' customer information, business data or accident records must not be used; where real food-safety judgements are involved, the rules of the unit and the competent authority must be followed.

values: Day 1: read one publicly available food-safety material

Using fictional refrigeration and heating temperature records, judge which period has abnormal readings and the possible direction of the cause, and explain your basis.

Write out the sequence for handling a temperature anomaly or a foreign object: stopping service, isolation, reporting, review and the conditions for resuming, and note which steps must be confirmed by authorised personnel.

Using a fictional order, write an isolation plan for allergen ingredients, utensils and workstations, and how you would explain it to service staff.
Day 6: write an end-of-shift handover
Using fictional data, write an end-of-shift record covering output, discards and temperature-control data, unresolved exceptions and the items the next shift needs to confirm.

Return to the judgement checklist on this page and write down three reasons you are willing to continue and two conditions that need caution.

entries: Concrete change: can you, given orders and temperature-control conditions, write out the conditions for stopping service, isolation and resuming, rather than just writing “pay attention to hygiene”.

Next step: if you are willing to continue with the previous six steps, the next step is, subject to compliance (for example a cooking course, in-company training or an open-kitchen experience), to complete one full loop from receiving and prep through heating to service and an end-of-shift record, and have an experienced cook review it; if a particular step clearly drains you, narrow the direction first and then verify.

The growth rate is a relative change over the projection period; the net change in headcount over the same period and average annual openings are different measures and cannot substitute for one another.

subject.summary: Cooks (occupational family) is the combined page for the U.S. SOC 35-2010 cook family, covering fast food, institution and cafeteria, private household, restaurant, short order and all other cooks: receiving and preparing ingredients, weighing, cutting and heating according to recipes, orders and food-safety conditions, monitoring temperature and doneness, portioning and plating and coordinating service, then cleaning equipment, storing ingredients and recording inventory; on the Chinese side the Chinese cuisine chef (occupation code 4-03-02-01) and similar entities are checked separately, and the two classifications do not correspond one-to-one.
